tagline.text: A World War II Japanese underground tunnel and Japanese-style garden beneath an Ilagan hill

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Santo Tomas, Ilagan City, Isabela

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–400 (per person, half day, covering admission, rentals and a light meal; transport not included)

children.text: The Ilagan Japanese Tunnel is a World War II tunnel about 40 m long in Santo Tomas, Ilagan City, Isabela, restored and opened to the public on February 16, 2016. Combine the tunnel exhibits with the Japanese-style garden on the hill and a kimono photo session for a half-day history stop.

The Ilagan Japanese Tunnel lies in Barangay Santo Tomas, Ilagan City, the capital of Isabela province in the Cagayan Valley of northern Luzon. It is a hand-dug tunnel, not a natural cave, which the Japanese army built as part of a military headquarters complex during the Japanese occupation, between

. According to the City of Ilagan's tourism information and local travel accounts, the Japanese forced detained local residents to dig it, used it to store bombs, explosives, guns and ammunition, and imprisoned and tortured captured Filipino guerrillas there. Although it is now a tourist attraction, it remains a historical site that carries painful memories of the occupation.

The tunnel was forgotten for a long time. One travel account says local children found the entrance while playing hide-and-seek, and village elders then began sharing what they had heard about it. The Ilagan city government decided to restore and preserve the site, and opened it to the public on
February 16, 2016
, during the term of Mayor Josemarie Diaz. The section open to visitors is about
long and about

wide and high. The full length of the tunnel has not been surveyed and remains unknown, and some residents believe similar tunnels run beneath the town. There are also stories of a larger tunnel in Barangay Camunatan, but it has not been found.

What sets this place apart from an ordinary tunnel visit is the Japanese-style landscaping on the hill above it. Past the ticket office and souvenir shop you reach a Japanese garden with a Shinto shrine-style structure, a small bridge, wind chimes (furin) and a koi pond. A stairway cut into the hillside climbs to a watchtower, with torii gates at the bottom and top. Life-size concrete statues of Japanese soldiers stand inside and outside the tunnel, and a children's playground, a treehouse and picnic tables make it popular with families.
In short, the Ilagan Japanese Tunnel is a good stop of about
2–3 hours

on the road between Tuguegarao and Cauayan. It is not a large site, but the darkness of the tunnel, the exhibits and the Japanese-themed photo spots are all in one place, which makes it a memorable stop on an Isabela trip. Fees and opening hours differ slightly between sources, so they are given below as ranges. Check the latest information with the city tourism office or the tunnel's Facebook page before you go.

blocks.title: About 40 m of Japanese military tunnel

children.text: The open section of the tunnel is about
long and about
wide and high. Inside, it is divided into chambers that were used as offices and quarters, and chambers said to have served as cells for prisoners. The air is dark and cool.

Displays include defused bomb shells, Japanese rifles, uniforms, machine guns and ammunition, along with replica golden Buddhas, gold bars and a golden fan. Items donated by veterans, historians and local residents are also said to be on show. According to visitor accounts, photography is not allowed inside the tunnel but is allowed outside.
The garden has a shrine-style structure, a small bridge, a koi pond and wind chimes. Hanging a wind chime to make a wish is reported to cost around
, and photos holding a Japanese-style umbrella are popular.
A stairway up the hillside leads to a watchtower, said to have been used to watch for attacks from the air and ground. The torii gates at the bottom and top of the stairs make good photo backdrops.
Kimono can reportedly be rented for around
, with men's and children's options available. Some accounts also mention geisha-style hairstyling and Japanese umbrellas for women visitors, so ask on site.

blocks.title: Soldier statues and a plane model

children.text: Life-size concrete statues of Japanese soldiers stand inside and outside the tunnel. There are also installations such as a model of a Japanese World War II plane with a broken wing, which conveys the atmosphere of the war visually.
There is a children's playground, a treehouse and picnic tables, and a food court that is said to serve Japanese food. The city's tourism itineraries also include lunch at this food court.

According to visitor accounts, around the anniversary every February, Japanese tea is served free, admission is halved and performances are held. This may change from year to year, so confirm the schedule with the tunnel.

Arrive at Bonifacio Park in Ilagan City. The tourist information center in this roadside park can arrange a guide to take you to the tunnel. The park's rotunda holds the giant armchair known as the Giant Butaka, built in 2003 to promote Isabela's furniture industry, which makes a good first photo stop.
Head to the tunnel in Santo Tomas by tricycle or private car. It is about
6.5 km
from the Provincial Capitol, roughly
15 minutes
by car.
Buy a ticket at the ticket office and explore the tunnel. It is dark inside and photography is restricted, so it is easiest to see the inside first and take photos outside afterward.
Climb the hillside stairs to the watchtower and torii gates, then stroll through the garden, koi pond and wind chime area. If you are renting a kimono for photos, fit it in at this time.
Have lunch at the food court and finish up. If you have time left, you can continue to other attractions in Ilagan.

The city tourism office's city-tour itineraries follow a similar order: Bonifacio Park, the tunnel, then lunch at the tunnel food court. One travel writer found a one-hour visit too short and recommended staying longer than an hour.

items.title: From Ilagan town to the tunnel

children.text: You can arrange a guide to the tunnel at the tourist information center in Bonifacio Park.
The tunnel is about
6.5 km
from the Provincial Capitol, roughly
15 minutes
by car. Tricycles are widely used in town. Fares depend on distance and negotiation, so check locally.
In a map app, search for the coordinates 17.1405, 121.8876 or the Plus Code 4VRQ+328.

The tunnel combines indoor and outdoor sections, so you can visit on a rainy day, but the garden and stairs get slippery when wet. The Cagayan Valley is affected by typhoons at certain times of year, so it is best to pick a clear day.
Every February, anniversary events for the tunnel are reported, with free Japanese tea, half-price admission and performances. Exact dates and programs may differ from year to year, so check locally.

There is no lodging at the tunnel itself, so most visitors stay in Ilagan town or Cauayan City. Ilagan is the provincial capital of Isabela and has hotels and guesthouses in town, and you can also stay in Tuguegarao and make a half-day trip. Room rates and conditions change often, so check recent reviews on a booking app.

The food court at the tunnel is the closest place to eat. Visitor accounts and tourism information describe a food court serving Japanese dishes such as ramen, takoyaki, gyoza and maki. We could not confirm the menu or prices, so please check on site. Ilagan town has Filipino restaurants and fast-food outlets, so you have plenty of choices.
Stop by the tourist information center at Bonifacio Park first to get a guide and up-to-date information.
Many visitors say the tunnel is dark, so bring a phone flashlight and go in with a companion.
Visitor accounts say photography is prohibited inside the tunnel, so check at the entrance and follow the rule. Photography is allowed outside.
Wear closed, non-slip shoes with low heels. The tunnel floor and stairs get slippery when wet.
If you want Japanese-style photos, ask as soon as you arrive whether kimono are available to rent.
Filming and wedding photo shoots are said to require separate registration with set fees. Apply first at the souvenir shop before shooting.
Check by phone or Facebook before you go that the site is open. Visitor accounts list the tunnel's contact numbers as 0935-701-1586 and 0932-858-3081.
Visitor accounts mention a separate fee for restroom use, so carry small change.
Opening hours and fees differ between sources (hours from
to

The tunnel is narrow and dark with little air movement, so it may not suit people who are claustrophobic or have limited mobility. We could not confirm wheelchair or stroller access, so ask the tourism office.
This is a historical site where forced labor and torture took place during the war. Do not make noise or touch the exhibits, and follow your guide's instructions.
The story that Yamashita treasure is buried in the tunnel is only a local belief, not a confirmed fact.
The garden structures were built for tourism. Not everything Japanese-style is a relic from the period, so keep the two apart.
Roads and stairs are slippery in the rainy season, and the site may close during typhoons, so check weather information.
A giant wooden armchair at the rotunda in Bonifacio Park, Ilagan. It was unveiled on April 23, 2003, stands about
(11.4 ft) tall and weighs about 2.4 tons, and promotes Isabela's furniture industry. It is a good stop on the way to the tunnel.

A park of about 200 hectares in Barangay Santa Victoria at the foot of the Sierra Madre, part of Fuyot Springs National Park. It is described as having caves, a waterfall and a zipline, and lies about
15 km
from town.
